'''''Arrhenatherum elatius''''' is a species of [[flowering plant]] in the grass family [[Poaceae]], commonly known as '''false oat-grass''',<ref name=Plantatlas>[https://plantatlas2020.org/atlas/2cd4p9h.v7t False Oat-grass] at [https://plantatlas2020.org/ Plant Atlas 2020]</ref> and also '''bulbous oat grass''' (subsp. ''bulbosum''),<ref name = GRIN>{{GRIN}}</ref> '''tall oat-grass''', '''tall meadow oat''', '''onion couch''' and '''tuber oat-grass'''. It is native throughout Europe (including Iceland), and also western and southwestern Asia (south to Jordan and Iran), and northwestern Africa (Morocco to Tunisia).<ref name=powo>{{cite web |title=''Arrhenatherum elatius'' (L.) P.Beauv. ex J.Presl & C.Presl |work=Plants of the World Online |publisher=Kew Science |url=https://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/urn:lsid:ipni.org:names:389923-1 |access-date=9 June 2020}}</ref> This [[Tussock grass|tufted grass]]<ref name=Plantatlas/> is sometimes used as an [[ornamental grass]]{{citation needed|date=June 2024}} and is sometimes marketed as "[[cat grass]]".{{citation needed|date=June 2023}}

Outside of its native range it can be found elsewhere as an [[introduced species]].<ref name=powo/> It is found especially in [[prairie]]s, at the side of roads and in uncultivated fields. The bulbous subspecies can be a weed of [[arable land]]. It is palatable grass for [[livestock]] and is used both as [[forage]] (pasture) and [[fodder]] ([[hay]] and [[silage]]).

==Description==

This coarse grass can grow to {{convert|1.80|m|ft|abbr=on|0}} tall.<ref name = "Streeter">Streeter D, Hart-Davies C, Hardcastle A, Cole F, Harper L. 2009. ''Collins Flower Guide''. Harper Collins {{ISBN|9-78-000718389-0}}</ref> The leaves are {{convert|4–10|mm|in|abbr=on|0}} wide, bright green, broad, slightly hairy, and rough. The [[ligule]] is {{convert|1–3|mm|in|abbr=on|0}} long and smooth edged.<ref name = "Streeter"/> The [[panicle]] is up to {{convert|30|cm|in|abbr=on|0}}, and the bunched [[spikelet]]s have projecting and angled [[Awn (botany)|awns]] up to {{convert|17|mm|in|abbr=on|0}} long, green or purplish. The panicles often remain into winter.<ref>[http://www.bsbi.org.uk/identification.html BSBI Description] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110717004923/http://www.bsbi.org.uk/identification.html |date=2011-07-17 }} retrieved 10 December 2010.</ref> The [[spikelet]]s are oblong or gaping. It flowers from June to September.  The roots are yellow.<ref>Grasses by C E Hubbard, 1978, published by Penguin books</ref>

Four subspecies are currently accepted by Kew's ''Plants of the World'':<ref name=powo/>
* ''Arrhenatherum elatius'' subsp. ''elatius'', the typical (nominate) subspecies.
* ''Arrhenatherum elatius'' subsp. ''bulbosum'' ([[Synonym (taxonomy)|syn.]] ''Arrhenatherum tuberosum''), onion couch or tuber oat-grass, distinguished by the presence of corms at the base of the stem, by which it propagates. It occurs in [[vegetated shingle]] and arable land.<ref name=Stace>{{cite book|last=Stace|first=C. A.|author-link = Stace, C. A.|year=2019|title=New Flora of the British Isles|edition=Fourth|publisher=C & M Floristics|location=Middlewood Green, Suffolk, U.K.| isbn=978-1-5272-2630-2}}</ref>{{rp|1065}}
* ''Arrhenatherum elatius'' subsp. ''cypricola'' ([[Cyprus]], [[endemism|endemic]]).
* ''Arrhenatherum elatius'' subsp. ''sardoum'' (western Mediterranean region).

==Habitat==

''Arrhenatherum elatius'' is a principal species in two UK [[British National Vegetation Classification|National Vegetation Classification]] habitat communities: the very widespread [[British NVC community MG1|MG1 (''Arrhenatherum elatius'' grassland)]] and the much rarer [[British NVC community MG2|MG2 (''Arrhenatherum elatius'' - ''Filipendula ulmaria'' tall-herb grassland)]]. This means that it can be found with species such as ''[[Dactylis glomerata]]'' (also known as cock's-foot and orchard grass), and ''[[Filipendula ulmaria]]'' (also known as meadow-sweet).

It is found on road verges, along hedges and riverbanks.

It can colonise and stabilise limestone scree, bare calcareous cliffs, maritime shingle and coastal dunes.
